title: Introduction to Git and Github
text:
Introduction to Git and Github
Git and GitHub are the tools data scientists use to track changes to their work, recover earlier versions, and collaborate without overwriting each other. This book is a hands-on introduction, built around a single running example that grows from an empty folder into a shared repository on GitHub.

title: Introduction to Git and Github
text:
Where these materials come from
These materials are based on the Version Control with Git video series produced by the UW-Madison Data Science Facilitators at the Data Science Institute. We are grateful for their work.
The book is designed as an alternative to watching the videos: the same material, in a form you can read quickly, follow along with during a workshop, and return to later when a specific question comes up — without scrubbing through an hour of video to find the one command you need.
Where it helps, we have also updated the workflows to use current Git commands:

To restore a previous version of a file, we use git restore rather than the older git checkout.
To move between branches, we use git switch rather than git checkout.

These newer commands each do one job, which makes them clearer and harder to misuse than the older, overloaded git checkout.


How this book is organized
The book has seven units plus a few reference appendices.

Units 1–5 are the core everyday workflow. They are covered live in a one-hour, hands-on workshop.
Units 6–7 (Conflicts and Branches) go beyond the live hour and are here for you to explore on your own afterward.

Every unit also has a companion slide deck, published on Posit Connect Cloud (Units 1–5 are the decks we present live):



Unit
Slide deck




1 — Introduction and Setup
open deck


2 — Tracking Changes
open deck


3 — Exploring History
open deck


4 — Ignoring Files
open deck


5 — Remotes in GitHub
open deck


6 — Conflicts
open deck


7 — Branches
open deck



The appendices cover one-time setup you should finish before the workshop — installing Git on Windows (Windows users only) and connecting to GitHub with SSH keys — and a cheatsheet at the end collects every command in one place for quick reference.


How to use this book
Git is best learned by doing. As you read, follow along in a terminal — Git Bash on Windows, or Terminal on macOS/Linux, or even the terminal in RStudio — and type the commands yourself. Everything builds one running example (Bucky Badger’s game-day menu), so the repository you create grows right alongside the book.
A few conventions to know:

Commands you type appear in shaded code blocks, with the output Git prints shown just below them.
Your turn boxes are short challenges to try on your own before moving on.
Keep the cheatsheet open in another tab for quick reference.

The source for this book lives on GitHub; corrections and suggestions are welcome.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.1 Why are we here?
By the end of this hour you will be able to:
We will build one project together, start to finish: Bucky’s game-day menu.
You’ll build this repo along with me the whole hour — including the Your turn moments, where you try a step on your own before we regroup.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
Explain what version control is and why it matters for data science
Put a project folder under Git and track changes to it
Save versions with meaningful messages, and look back at your history
Tell Git to ignore files it should not track
Push your work to GitHub to back it up and share it

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.2 What is version control?
Version control keeps track of changes you make to files over time.



It lets you:

Go back to any earlier version of a file
Keep only one copy in your folder (not ten copies with different names)
See what changed, when, and why
Work with others without emailing files back and forth
Keep the same project synced across computers

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
section: 1.3 You have probably done this the hard way
text:
1.3 You have probably done this the hard way
How many of these folders have you lived in?



analysis.R
analysis_v2.R
analysis_final.R
analysis_final_FINAL.R
analysis_2026-10-01.R
analysis_2026-10-01_jjc.R



You cannot tell what changed between any two of them, and they all pile up in the same folder.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.4 Git fixes this
With Git, you keep one analysis.R in your folder.



Git quietly stores the full history behind the scenes. At any point you can:

Ask “what did this file look like last Tuesday?”
Read the note you left yourself explaining each change
Restore an older version without losing your current work





“Your closest collaborator is you six months ago, and they don’t answer email.”

Git is how you leave notes for that person.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.5 Git is not GitHub
A point of confusion worth clearing up right away:









What it is


Where it lives






Git


The version-control software


On your computer




GitHub


A website that hosts Git repositories


In the cloud







You can use Git with no internet at all. GitHub is where you put a copy to back it up, share it, and collaborate. We get there at the end of the hour.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
section: 1.6 Our running example: Bucky’s game-day menu
text:
1.6 Our running example: Bucky’s game-day menu
Bucky Badger is planning the food for a game-day tailgate, and the menu keeps changing.



We will keep the plan in a folder called gameday-menu, with a file per part of the spread:

brats.txt
cheese_curds.txt
desserts.txt




As the menu evolves, we will use Git to track every change, so Bucky can always see what the plan looked like last week.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.7 What you should already have
This lecture assumes three things are done:

Git is installed on your laptop
You have a GitHub account
You have an SSH key set up to validate your idenity with Github




If these are not yet done, see Appendices A & B now, and then catch up with a neighbor:

https://carpentries.github.io/workshop-template/#git




Everything today happens in a terminal (Git Bash on Windows; Terminal on macOS/Linux). Git commands all start with the word git.



RStudio also has a built in terminal. I use it rather than a separate terminal for git and file management when I am working on analysis code for a project. Its up to you!

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.8 Tell Git who you are
Git stamps every saved version with a name and email. Set yours once per computer:



git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@wisc.edu"



Use your own name and email, not Bucky’s. The email should match the one on your GitHub account.
The --global flag means “use this for every project on this computer,” so you only do it once.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.9 Check that it worked
You can confirm your settings at any time:



git config --list



Look for your user.name and user.email in the output:
user.name=Bucky Badger
user.email=bucky@wisc.edu
init.defaultBranch=main



If you made a typo, just run the config command again to overwrite it.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
section: 1.10 Make a folder for the project
text:
1.10 Make a folder for the project
Create a folder for Bucky’s menu and move into it.



I prefer to keep all of my git repos at one location (~/github)



cd
mkdir github
cd github

mkdir gameday-menu
cd gameday-menu



Right now this is just an ordinary folder. Git is not watching it yet.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
section: 1.11 Turn the folder into a repository
text:
1.11 Turn the folder into a repository
A repository (or “repo”) is a folder that Git is tracking, along with its full history.



Turn the current folder into one with a single command:
git init



Initialized empty Git repository in /home/github/gameday-menu/.git/



Git created a hidden .git folder to store the history. You never edit it by hand; Git manages it for you.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.12 Meet git status
git status is the command you will run the most. It tells you where things stand.



git status



On branch main
No commits yet
nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.13 Reading that message
Three things Git just told us:




On branch main — the default line of work (more on branches another day)
No commits yet — we have no saved history in this repo
nothing to commit — the folder is empty, so there is nothing to track




Notice the hint: use “git add” to track. Git is telling us the next step.

title: 1  Introduction and Setup
text:
1.14 Where we are
We have:

Confirmed Git knows who we are
Created the gameday-menu folder
Turned it into a Git repository with git init
Learned to check in with git status











ImportantNext up



Bucky still has no food on the menu. Next we will create our first files and learn how Git saves versions of them with add and commit.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.1 The rhythm of Git
Every version you save follows the same two-step rhythm:
Along the way, three commands let you check in:

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
Edit your files as usual
git add — mark the changes you want to save
git commit — save them as a point in history






git status — where do things stand?
git diff — what exactly changed?
git log — what have I saved so far?

title: 2  Tracking Changes
section: 2.2 Put the first item on the menu
text:
2.2 Put the first item on the menu
Bucky starts with the main event. Open a new file with nano:
nano brats.txt



Type one line, then save and exit with Ctrl+X, then Y, then Enter:
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill



Prefer a different editor? Open the file in the RStudio source editor, or use another terminal editor like vim (my preferred editor) — any of them works. These slides use nano. Either way, nothing has been handed to Git yet; we have only written to the folder.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.3 A new, untracked file
Check in with git status:
git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    brats.txt

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)



Git sees brats.txt but calls it untracked — it is not yet part of the history.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
section: 2.4 Step 1 of 2: stage it with git add
text:
2.4 Step 1 of 2: stage it with git add
Tell Git this file belongs in the next saved version:
git add brats.txt



This puts brats.txt on the stage — the group of changes that will be saved together on your next commit.



git add produces no output when it succeeds. Run git status to see what it did.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.5 Staged and ready
git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
    new file:   brats.txt



Now Git lists brats.txt under Changes to be committed. It is staged, but not yet saved to history.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
section: 2.6 Step 2 of 2: save it with git commit
text:
2.6 Step 2 of 2: save it with git commit
A commit is a permanent point in your history. It needs a short message describing the change:
git commit -m "Add brats to the menu"
[main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add brats to the menu
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 brats.txt



The -m flag supplies the message. This is our first commit, so Git labels it the root-commit and stamps it with a unique ID (a1b2c3d).

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.7 Working tree clean
git status
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean



Working tree clean means the folder matches the saved history exactly — nothing is waiting to be saved.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.8 Where your work lives
That two-step dance makes sense once you see the three places your work can be:







Working directory


Staging area


Repository






Your files as you edit them


Changes you have marked to save


The permanent history of commits







Two commands move your work to the right along this path.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
section: 2.9 git add moves work to the stage
text:
2.9 git add moves work to the stage




Working directory


Staging area


Repository






Your files as you edit them


Changes you have marked to save


The permanent history of commits







git add copies changes from your working directory onto the stage. You choose exactly what goes on.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.10 git commit records the stage




Working directory


Staging area


Repository






Your files as you edit them


Changes you have marked to save


The permanent history of commits







git commit records everything on the stage as one point in history. The extra step is a feature: it lets you group related changes into a single, meaningful commit.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.11 See your history: git log
git log
commit a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Bucky Badger <bucky@wisc.edu>
Date:   Fri Oct 9 10:15:00 2026 -0500

    Add brats to the menu



Each commit records the full ID, who made it, when, and the message. HEAD marks where you are now.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.12 Bucky tweaks the brats
How many to buy? Reopen the file:
nano brats.txt



Add a second line, then save and exit:
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)



Save the file, then check what Git thinks.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.13 A tracked file, now modified
git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
    modified:   brats.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")



This time Git already knows brats.txt, so it reports it as modified rather than untracked.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.14 What exactly changed? git diff
Came back from the stadium and forgot what you edited? Ask Git:
git diff brats.txt
diff --git a/brats.txt b/brats.txt
index 83db48f..f735c2d 100644
--- a/brats.txt
+++ b/brats.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
+Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)




Git colors the output: added lines show in green with a +, and removed lines would show in red with a -.

Prefer a visual, side-by-side diff? The Using Meld for Diffs appendix sets up git difftool to open these comparisons in Meld.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.15 Stage and commit the edit
Same two steps as before:
git add brats.txt
git commit -m "Note how many brats to buy"
[main b2c3d4e] Note how many brats to buy
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)



That is the whole rhythm: edit → add → commit. You will do it hundreds of times.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.16 One commit, two new files
The menu grows. Create two more files, one at a time:
nano cheese_curds.txt
Fried cheese curds from the Union - 2 baskets
nano desserts.txt
Babcock ice cream - chocolate and Union Blend



git status
Untracked files:
    cheese_curds.txt
    desserts.txt

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.17 Stage both at once
These two go together, so stage them in one step:
git add cheese_curds.txt desserts.txt



Preview what is staged with git diff --staged (plain git diff looks only at unstaged changes):
git diff --staged
diff --git a/cheese_curds.txt b/cheese_curds.txt
new file mode 100644
@@ -0,0 +1 @@
+Fried cheese curds from the Union - 2 baskets
diff --git a/desserts.txt b/desserts.txt
new file mode 100644
@@ -0,0 +1 @@
+Babcock ice cream - chocolate and Union Blend

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.18 Commit them together
Both new files land in one commit:
git commit -m "Add cheese curds and desserts"
[main c3d4e5f] Add cheese curds and desserts
 2 files changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 cheese_curds.txt
 create mode 100644 desserts.txt



This is why add and commit are separate steps: you decide what belongs together.



Later, we will learn how to undo a commit so best to stage and commit edits that represent some block of changes that belong together for some goal in your development/analysis workflow

title: 2  Tracking Changes
section: 2.19 The story so far: git log --oneline
text:
2.19 The story so far: git log --oneline
Full git log gets long fast. The --oneline flag gives one row per commit:
git log --oneline
c3d4e5f (HEAD -> main) Add cheese curds and desserts
b2c3d4e Note how many brats to buy
a1b2c3d Add brats to the menu



You can also limit the count: git log -2 shows just the two most recent commits.



Name a file to see only the commits that changed it — handy when you need to track down an error in one file:
git log --oneline brats.txt
b2c3d4e Note how many brats to buy
a1b2c3d Add brats to the menu



The cheese curds and desserts commit drops out — it never touched brats.txt. (Add -- before the name, git log --oneline -- brats.txt, if Git confuses it with a branch.)

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.20 Writing good commit messages
Your future self reads these. Aim for the middle ground:







Message


Verdict






changes


Too vague — says nothing




Added “Fried cheese curds from the Union - 2 baskets” to cheese_curds.txt


Too verbose — just repeats the file




Add cheese curds and desserts


Captures the meaning, briefly







Keep the first line under about 50 characters and describe the change, not the literal text.

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.21 Your turn







ImportantTry it



Bucky wants cream puffs. On your own:

Add a line to desserts.txt for cream puffs
Check what changed with git diff
Stage it with git add, then git commit with a clear message
Confirm it landed with git log --oneline

title: 2  Tracking Changes
text:
2.22 Where we are
We can now build history on purpose:

git add stages changes; git commit saves them
git status shows where things stand
git diff shows what changed; git log shows what we saved











ImportantNext up



Bucky commits a menu change he regrets. Next we will use the history to look back and restore an earlier version of a file.

title: 3  Exploring History
text:
3.1 The menu so far
Bucky has a few commits of history to work with:
Your commit IDs will differ from these, and you may also see your cream-puffs commit from the last exercise — all expected.
History is only useful if you can look back at it and recover from mistakes. That is what this unit is about.

title: 3  Exploring History
text:
git log --oneline
c3d4e5f (HEAD -> main) Add cheese curds and desserts
b2c3d4e Note how many brats to buy
a1b2c3d Add brats to the menu

title: 3  Exploring History
section: 3.2 Bucky makes a change he’ll regret
text:
3.2 Bucky makes a change he’ll regret
Late at night, Bucky second-guesses the whole plan. Open brats.txt:
nano brats.txt



Add a regrettable third line, then save and exit:
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)
Swap the brats for a kale salad



In the cold light of game day, this was a mistake. We want the old brats.txt back.

title: 3  Exploring History
section: 3.3 HEAD points to your latest commit
text:
3.3 HEAD points to your latest commit
HEAD is Git’s name for the commit you are currently on — normally your most recent one.



You can count backward from it:

HEAD — the latest commit
HEAD~1 — one commit before that
HEAD~2 — two commits before that




HEAD~1, HEAD~2, … are easy for recent commits. To reach a specific commit further back, copy its ID from git log --oneline rather than counting.

title: 3  Exploring History
text:
3.4 Review before you restore
Good practice: look at what you are about to throw away. Compare your file to the last commit:
git diff HEAD brats.txt
diff --git a/brats.txt b/brats.txt
index f735c2d..a9c3e21 100644
--- a/brats.txt
+++ b/brats.txt
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
 Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
 Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)
+Swap the brats for a kale salad




The only difference from the last commit is the one regrettable line. Safe to discard.

title: 3  Exploring History
section: 3.5 Undo an uncommitted change: git restore
text:
3.5 Undo an uncommitted change: git restore
Throw away the edit and bring back the committed version:
git restore brats.txt



git restore prints nothing on success. Check the result:
cat brats.txt
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)



The kale line is gone, and git status reports a clean working tree again.

title: 3  Exploring History
section: 3.6 How git restore picks what to bring back
text:
3.6 How git restore picks what to bring back
git restore reads a file from a source and writes it into your working directory.




By default the source is the staging area — which matches your last commit unless you have staged something. That is what just undid the uncommitted edit.
Point it at any commit with --source (short: -s) to reach back into history.




It overwrites your current working copy with no undo, so review with git diff first.

title: 3  Exploring History
section: 3.7 Reach back to an older commit
text:
3.7 Reach back to an older commit
Bucky is curious what the very first, one-line menu looked like. Find that commit’s ID at the bottom of your log:
git log --oneline
...
a1b2c3d Add brats to the menu



Restore brats.txt from that commit — use your own ID (here, a1b2c3d):
git restore --source=a1b2c3d brats.txt
cat brats.txt
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill



Only the working copy changed; the staging area and history are untouched.

title: 3  Exploring History
section: 3.8 The older version is now an unstaged change
text:
3.8 The older version is now an unstaged change
Because the working copy no longer matches the last commit, Git flags it as modified:
git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
    modified:   brats.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")



Two choices from here:

Keep it: git add + git commit to make the old version the new latest
Change your mind: git restore brats.txt snaps back to HEAD




So we all stay in sync for the rest of the lecture, let’s all snap back to HEAD:
git restore brats.txt

title: 3  Exploring History
text:
3.9 Your turn







ImportantTry it




Add a silly line to cheese_curds.txt with nano
Preview it with git diff HEAD cheese_curds.txt
Discard it with git restore cheese_curds.txt
Peek at the original brats: copy the Add brats to the menu ID from git log --oneline, run git restore --source=<that ID> brats.txt, cat it, then git restore brats.txt to return to the latest

title: 3  Exploring History
text:
3.10 Where we are
We can now travel through our history:

HEAD, HEAD~1, … name past commits
git diff HEAD <file> reviews changes since the last commit
git restore <file> discards uncommitted edits (from the staging area)
git restore --source=<commit> <file> brings back an older version











ImportantNext up



Bucky’s folder is filling up with files he never wants to track — scratch notes and receipts. Next we will teach Git to ignore them.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.1 Not everything belongs in Git
Git is built for tracking the files you author. Some files are better left untracked:
Instead of eyeballing git status and carefully avoiding them, we can tell Git to ignore them for good.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
Scratch and throwaway files — temporary notes, drafts, scratch output
Large or raw data — bloats the repo and rarely changes
Binary files — Git can’t meaningfully diff a photo or .xlsx; it just stores a full copy each time
Secrets — API keys, passwords, credentials should never be committed

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.2 Bucky’s folder gets cluttered
Game-day prep leaves a mess: scratch files and a folder of receipt photos.
touch scratch.tmp shopping-draft.tmp
mkdir receipts
touch receipts/costco.jpg receipts/metcalfe.jpg



The .tmp files are throwaway scratch; the receipts/ photos are big, binary, and nobody needs them in the menu’s history.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.3 Git sees the clutter
git status
On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    receipts/
    scratch.tmp
    shopping-draft.tmp

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)



Git keeps nagging about files we never intend to track — and worse, we might commit them by accident.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.4 Create a .gitignore
Git reads a file named .gitignore and ignores anything that matches a pattern in it. Create one:
nano .gitignore



Add two patterns, then save and exit:
*.tmp
receipts/



*.tmp matches any file ending in .tmp; the trailing slash in receipts/ matches that whole folder and everything inside it.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.5 The clutter disappears
git status
On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    .gitignore

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)



The scratch files and receipts/ are gone from the list. The only thing Git still sees is .gitignore itself.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.6 Track the .gitignore itself
Commit .gitignore so the rules travel with the project:
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Ignore scratch files and receipts"
[main d4e5f6a] Ignore scratch files and receipts
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore



Tracking it means anyone who clones the repo — including future you on another computer — ignores the same files automatically.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.7 Ignored means ignored
New files that match keep getting ignored, with no extra work:
touch results.tmp
git status
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean



And if you try to add an ignored file, Git stops you:
git add scratch.tmp
The following paths are ignored by one of your .gitignore files:
scratch.tmp
hint: Use -f if you really want to add them.



That warning is a feature. If you ever truly need to track one, git add -f forces it.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.8 Common things to ignore
For data science projects, a .gitignore usually covers:




Secrets — .env, API keys, credential files
Large or raw data — data/, *.csv, *.parquet
Generated output — rendered reports, figures, caches
Tool cruft — .Rhistory, .RData, .Rproj.user/, __pycache__/




Many languages and editors publish starter .gitignore files you can copy from — GitHub even offers one when you create a repo.

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.9 Your turn







ImportantTry it



Bucky keeps a private budget spreadsheet in the folder:

Create it with touch budget.xlsx
Confirm Git sees it with git status
Add a pattern to .gitignore so Git ignores .xlsx files
Run git status again — it should be gone. Then git add and git commit your updated .gitignore

title: 4  Ignoring Files
text:
4.10 Where we are
Bucky’s repo now ignores the clutter:

.gitignore lists patterns for files Git should skip
Patterns like *.tmp and receipts/ match files and folders
We commit .gitignore so the rules are shared











ImportantNext up



So far everything lives only on Bucky’s laptop. Next we will push the menu to GitHub to back it up and share it.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
text:
5.1 Everything lives on one laptop
So far Bucky’s whole menu — files and history — exists only on his computer.
That is fragile:
The fix is a copy hosted online that we sync with. That is what GitHub is for.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
text:
If the laptop dies, the repo and its history are gone
Bucky can’t work on it from another machine
He can’t share it or collaborate with teammates

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
text:
5.2 GitHub hosts your repo
GitHub is a website that stores Git repositories in the cloud. (GitLab and Bitbucket do the same thing.)



A hosted copy gives you three things:

Backup — your work survives a dead laptop
Sync — the same project on your laptop, your lab machine, a server
Collaboration — teammates can see and contribute




Remember: Git is the tool on your computer; GitHub is a place to host what Git tracks.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
section: 5.3 SSH keys: how GitHub knows it’s you
text:
5.3 SSH keys: how GitHub knows it’s you
When you push work to GitHub, it has to be sure the push is really from you.



SSH keys are a matched pair:

A private key that stays secret on your laptop
A public key that you give to GitHub




GitHub matches the two so you never type a password. You set this up once per computer — and you did it before class, so we will just confirm it works.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
text:
5.4 Verify your connection
Ask GitHub whether it recognizes your key:
ssh -T git@github.com
Hi buckybadger! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.



That greeting means your key works and you’re ready to push. If you instead get a permission denied error, follow the SSH setup guide or grab a neighbor before we go on.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
section: 5.5 Make a home for it on GitHub
text:
5.5 Make a home for it on GitHub
In your browser, signed in to GitHub:




Click + (top right) → New repository
Name it gameday-menu to match the local folder
Leave it Public
Do not check “Add a README,” “.gitignore,” or a license
Click Create repository




We skip the README and friends because we already have a repo with history. Starting a second history on GitHub would just collide with ours.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
text:
5.6 Copy the SSH address
The new repo’s page shows setup hints. Find the SSH address (make sure the SSH tab is selected, not HTTPS):



git@github.com:buckybadger/gameday-menu.git



This is the address of your GitHub copy. We will hand it to Git so your laptop knows where to send things.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
section: 5.7 Point your repo at GitHub: git remote add
text:
5.7 Point your repo at GitHub: git remote add
A remote is a named connection to a hosted copy. Add one, using your own address:
git remote add origin git@github.com:buckybadger/gameday-menu.git



origin is the conventional name for your main remote. Confirm it:
git remote -v
origin  git@github.com:buckybadger/gameday-menu.git (fetch)
origin  git@github.com:buckybadger/gameday-menu.git (push)

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
text:
5.8 Send it up: git push
Push your main branch to the origin remote:
git push origin main
Enumerating objects: 12, done.
Writing objects: 100% (12/12), 1.1 KiB | 1.1 MiB/s, done.
To github.com:buckybadger/gameday-menu.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main



Reload the GitHub page: your files and every commit are now there. Note that receipts/ and the .tmp files are absent — they were ignored, so they never traveled.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
section: 5.9 The everyday loop: pull and push
text:
5.9 The everyday loop: pull and push
With a remote in place, syncing is two commands:




git pull origin main — bring down changes from GitHub (a teammate’s work, or edits from another machine)
git push origin main — send your new commits up




Good habit: pull when you start, push when you finish. And to get the repo onto a brand-new machine, git clone <address> creates the folder, sets up origin, and downloads everything in one step.

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
text:
5.10 Your turn







ImportantTry it



Make a change and publish it:

Add a line to desserts.txt with nano (kringle, for the Wisconsin touch)
git add and git commit with a clear message
git push origin main
Refresh your repo on GitHub and watch the new commit appear

title: 5  Remotes in GitHub
text:
5.11 Where we are
Bucky’s menu now lives on GitHub, backed up and shareable:

git remote add origin <address> links the local repo to GitHub
git push origin main sends commits up; git pull origin main brings them down
git clone <address> copies a repo onto a new machine











ImportantWhat’s next



Working with others means parallel changes — which brings branches and merge conflicts. Those live in the book chapters to explore on your own. Keep the cheatsheet handy.

title: 6  Conflicts
text:
6.1 When does a conflict happen?
A conflict happens when two commits change the same line of the same file in different ways, and Git can’t tell which one is right.
It usually surfaces when you bring two lines of work together — for us, when you git pull and someone else has edited the same line you did.
Conflicts are normal, not a disaster. Git just needs you, the human, to decide what the final version should say.

title: 6  Conflicts
section: 6.2 Our setup: two people, one repo
text:
6.2 Our setup: two people, one repo
Bucky’s menu is on GitHub. His co-organizer Sam clones it to help plan dessert.



To follow along on your own, clone a second copy into a different folder — it stands in for Sam’s computer:
cd ~/github
git clone git@github.com:buckybadger/gameday-menu.git gameday-menu-sam



Now there are two working copies of the same repo: your original gameday-menu and gameday-menu-sam.

title: 6  Conflicts
section: 6.3 Sam changes a line and pushes
text:
6.3 Sam changes a line and pushes
In Sam’s copy, edit the ice cream line in desserts.txt:
cd ~/github/gameday-menu-sam
nano desserts.txt
Babcock ice cream - Orange Custard Chocolate Chip



Then commit and push it up to GitHub:
git add desserts.txt
git commit -m "Pick Orange Custard Chocolate Chip ice cream"
git push origin main



GitHub now has Sam’s version of that line.

title: 6  Conflicts
section: 6.4 Meanwhile, you change the same line
text:
6.4 Meanwhile, you change the same line
Back in your original copy — not knowing what Sam did — edit the same line differently:
cd ~/github/gameday-menu
nano desserts.txt
Babcock ice cream - Union Blend
git add desserts.txt
git commit -m "Pick Union Blend ice cream"



Both commits look fine on their own. The trouble starts when they meet.

title: 6  Conflicts
text:
6.5 The push is rejected
Try to push your version:
git push origin main
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:buckybadger/gameday-menu.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally. Integrate the remote changes before pushing again.



GitHub is protecting Sam’s commit. It’s telling you to pull first and reconcile before you can push.

title: 6  Conflicts
section: 6.6 Pull brings the conflict to light
text:
6.6 Pull brings the conflict to light
git pull origin main
Auto-merging desserts.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in desserts.txt
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.



Git merged everything it could, but it can’t auto-merge that one line — you both rewrote it. It stops and hands the decision to you.

title: 6  Conflicts
section: 6.7 git status points you to the problem
text:
6.7 git status points you to the problem
git status
On branch main
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
    both modified:   desserts.txt



both modified is the tell-tale sign of a conflict. If you ever feel stuck, git merge --abort backs out and returns you to before the pull.

title: 6  Conflicts
text:
6.8 Reading the conflict markers
Open desserts.txt. Git has inserted markers around the clashing lines:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Babcock ice cream - Union Blend
=======
Babcock ice cream - Orange Custard Chocolate Chip
>>>>>>> 3f9a1c2 (Pick Orange Custard Chocolate Chip ice cream)




Between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your version
Between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming version from GitHub

title: 6  Conflicts
text:
6.9 Resolve it: you decide
Edit the file so it reads exactly how you want, and delete all three marker lines. Bucky wants both flavors:
Babcock ice cream - Union Blend and Orange Custard Chocolate Chip



You are free to keep your version, keep theirs, combine them, or write something new. Just make sure every marker (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) is gone — a file can have several conflicts, so check the whole thing.

title: 6  Conflicts
text:
6.10 Mark it resolved and commit
Once the markers are gone, stage the file to tell Git the conflict is settled, then commit:
git add desserts.txt
git commit -m "Merge: offer both ice cream flavors"
git push origin main



That commit records the resolution. Now push succeeds, and Sam can git pull to pick up the agreed-on version. The conflict is behind you.

title: 6  Conflicts
text:
6.11 Avoiding conflicts
You can’t prevent them entirely, but a few habits make them rare and small:




Pull before you start working, so you begin from the latest version
Push often, in small focused commits
Coordinate with collaborators about who is editing what




And when one does happen — read the markers, decide, delete them, add, commit. That’s the whole skill.

title: 6  Conflicts
text:
6.12 Your turn







ImportantTry it



Make a conflict on purpose and resolve it:

In gameday-menu-sam, change a line in brats.txt, commit, and push
In gameday-menu, change the same line differently and commit
git push (watch it get rejected), then git pull to trigger the conflict
Edit brats.txt to settle it, remove the markers, then git add, git commit, and git push

title: 6  Conflicts
text:
6.13 Where we are
Conflicts are a skill, not a catastrophe:

They arise when two commits change the same line
git pull surfaces them; both modified in git status flags them
Edit the file, remove the markers, then git add and git commit











ImportantNext up



The same conflict can happen when you merge branches — parallel lines of work in a single repo. That is the next unit.

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.1 Why branch?
A branch is a parallel line of work inside one repository. It lets you try something without touching your main version.
Branches are useful when you want to:
You’ve been on a branch the whole time — the default one, called main. Now we’ll make a second.

title: 7  Branches
text:
Experiment with a risky change while keeping a working version safe
Draft a feature that isn’t ready for everyone yet
Keep main stable while work is in progress

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.2 Where you are now
List the branches in your repo:
git branch
* main



The * (shown in color) marks the branch you’re currently on. There’s only one so far, and git status reminds you of it too (On branch main).

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.3 Bucky wants to experiment
Bucky is tempted to add a vegetarian spread to the menu — but he doesn’t want to disturb the plan that already works.



Perfect job for a branch: he can draft the veggie options off to the side, decide if he likes them, and only then bring them into main.

title: 7  Branches
section: 7.4 Create and switch in one step
text:
7.4 Create and switch in one step
Make a new branch and move onto it:
git switch -c veggie-option
Switched to a new branch 'veggie-option'



The -c flag creates the branch and switches to it. It starts as an exact copy of main’s history.



Confirm where you are:
git branch
  main
* veggie-option

To create a branch without switching, use git branch <name>. In older Git, git checkout -b does what git switch -c does here.

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.5 Work on the branch
Draft the vegetarian items in a new file:
nano veggie.txt
Grilled veggie skewers
Portobello "brats" for the vegetarians



Save it to history as usual — this commit lands on veggie-option, not main:
git add veggie.txt
git commit -m "Draft vegetarian options"

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.6 main is untouched
Switch back and look:
git switch main
ls
brats.txt  cheese_curds.txt  desserts.txt



No veggie.txt here — it lives only on the branch. main is exactly as you left it. That isolation is the whole point of branching.

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.7 See the branches diverge
A decorated, graphed log shows how the branches relate:
git log --oneline --all --graph
* 7a1b2c3 (veggie-option) Draft vegetarian options
* 1d2e3f4 (HEAD -> main) Ignore scratch files and receipts
* c3d4e5f Add cheese curds and desserts



--all shows every branch and --graph draws the structure. Here veggie-option sits one commit ahead of main.

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.8 Keep it? Merge into main
Bucky likes the veggie options, so he brings them into main. First be on the branch you’re merging into, then merge:
git switch main
git merge veggie-option
Updating 1d2e3f4..7a1b2c3
Fast-forward
 veggie.txt | 2 ++
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)



main had no new commits of its own, so Git just fast-forwards it to catch up. veggie.txt is now part of main.

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.9 Clean up the branch
Once a branch is merged, delete it to keep things tidy:
git branch -d veggie-option
Deleted branch veggie-option (was 7a1b2c3).



If a branch is not fully merged, -d refuses and warns you — so you don’t lose work by accident. git branch -D (capital D) force-deletes when you really mean it.

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.10 When merges collide
Our merge was clean because main hadn’t changed. But if main and your branch both edited the same line, Git can’t fast-forward — the merge stops with a conflict.



You already know how to handle it: open the file, remove the <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> markers, keep what you want, then git add and git commit. (See the Conflicts unit.)

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.11 Your turn







ImportantTry it



Branch, work, merge, clean up:

From main, run git switch -c dessert-upgrade
Add a line to desserts.txt, then git add and git commit
git switch main and confirm the change isn’t there yet
git merge dessert-upgrade, then git branch -d dessert-upgrade

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.12 Where we are
Branches let you work in parallel safely:

git branch lists branches; git switch -c <name> creates and moves onto one
Commits land on the current branch, leaving main safe
git merge <branch> brings the work together; git branch -d cleans up











ImportantKeep going



On GitHub, branches power pull requests — the standard way to propose and review changes with collaborators. That’s a great next thing to explore, with the cheatsheet at your side.

title: Appendix A — Installing Git for Windows
text:
A.1 Download the installer
This appendix is for students on Windows. It installs Git for Windows, which bundles both Git and the Bash shell into a single program called Git Bash — the terminal we use throughout these lessons. Plan on about ten minutes, and do it before the live session.
Go to gitforwindows.org and download the installer. Once it finishes, double-click the downloaded .exe to start.

title: Appendix A — Installing Git for Windows
text:
A.2 Run the installer
The installer has many screens. You can accept the defaults on nearly all of them — just click Next through to the end. Four screens are worth stopping for, because they match how we work in class:

Choosing the default editor used by Git — from the dropdown, select Use the Nano editor by default. (You may need to scroll up to find it.) Our lessons write commit messages in nano.
Adjusting the name of the initial branch in new repositories — choose Override the default branch name and type main. This matches the branch name we use everywhere in these materials.
Adjusting your PATH environment — keep the recommended Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software. If you miss this, Git Bash won’t work properly with other tools.
Configuring the line ending conversions — keep Checkout Windows-style, commit Unix-style line endings.

For every other screen — OpenSSH, the HTTPS backend, the terminal emulator, credential manager, and so on — the default is fine. Click Install, then Finish.

title: Appendix A — Installing Git for Windows
section: A.3 Open Git Bash and check
text:
A.3 Open Git Bash and check
Open the Start menu, type Git Bash, and open it. You’ll get a terminal window. Confirm Git is installed:
git --version
git version 2.46.0.windows.1
A version number means you’re set. This Git Bash window gives you both Git and Bash — it is the terminal you’ll use to follow along in class.

title: Appendix A — Installing Git for Windows
section: A.4 If Git Bash can’t find your home folder
text:
A.4 If Git Bash can’t find your home folder
Occasionally ~ (your home folder) isn’t set correctly. If commands that use ~ misbehave, open the Windows Command Prompt (Start menu → type cmd) and run:
setx HOME "%USERPROFILE%"
You should see SUCCESS: Specified value was saved. Close and reopen Git Bash.

title: Appendix A — Installing Git for Windows
text:
A.5 Next steps
With Git Bash installed, you’re ready to:

Set your name and email, covered in the Introduction and Setup unit
Connect to GitHub, covered in the Setting Up SSH Keys appendix

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
text:
B.1 What SSH keys do
This appendix walks through connecting your computer to GitHub with SSH keys. You do this once per computer, before you need to push to GitHub (the Remotes in GitHub unit). Set aside about ten minutes.
If you have already set up SSH keys on this machine and ssh -T git@github.com greets you by name, you can skip this guide.
When you push work to GitHub, it needs to confirm the push is really from you. SSH keys handle that without a password. A key is a matched pair:
GitHub matches the public key you gave it against the private key on your machine. If they pair up, you’re in. You generate the pair once, register the public half with GitHub, and from then on git push and git pull just work.
Everything below happens in a terminal: Git Bash on Windows, or Terminal on macOS/Linux.

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
text:
A private key that stays secret on your computer — never share it.
A public key that you hand to GitHub.

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
section: B.2 Step 1: Check for an existing key
text:
B.2 Step 1: Check for an existing key
You may already have a key from other work. Look for one:
ls -al ~/.ssh
If you see a file named id_ed25519.pub (or id_rsa.pub), you already have a key pair and can skip to Step 4. If the folder is empty or does not exist, continue to Step 2.

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
section: B.3 Step 2: Generate a new key
text:
B.3 Step 2: Generate a new key
Create a key, substituting the email tied to your GitHub account:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@wisc.edu"
ed25519 is a modern, secure key type. The command then asks you two things:

File in which to save the key: press Enter to accept the default location (~/.ssh/id_ed25519).
Passphrase: type a passphrase and press Enter, then type it again to confirm. A passphrase protects the key if someone ever copies it off your machine.

One thing that surprises people: as you type the passphrase, the terminal shows nothing — no dots, no cursor movement. That is normal. If you lose track, press Backspace several times and start again.
When it finishes, you have two files: id_ed25519 (private — keep secret) and id_ed25519.pub (public — safe to share).

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
section: B.4 Step 3 (optional): Avoid retyping your passphrase
text:
B.4 Step 3 (optional): Avoid retyping your passphrase
If you would rather not enter your passphrase on every push, add the key to the SSH agent:
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
This is convenient but optional. You can skip it and simply type your passphrase when prompted.

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
section: B.5 Step 4: Copy your public key
text:
B.5 Step 4: Copy your public key
Print the public key and copy the entire line, from ssh-ed25519 through your email:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAI...rest-of-key... you@wisc.edu
Only ever copy the .pub file. The matching file without .pub is your private key and should never leave your computer.






Note



Shortcut to copy straight to your clipboard:

macOS: pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Windows (Git Bash): clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Linux: xclip -sel clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
section: B.6 Step 5: Add the key to GitHub
text:
B.6 Step 5: Add the key to GitHub
In your browser, signed in to GitHub:

Click your profile photo (top right) → Settings
In the left sidebar, choose SSH and GPG keys
Click New SSH key
Give it a Title that names the computer (e.g., “Work laptop”)
Leave the key type as Authentication Key, paste your public key into the Key box
Click Add SSH key

Your key now appears in the list.

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
text:
B.7 Step 6: Test the connection
Back in your terminal, ask GitHub whether it recognizes you:
ssh -T git@github.com
The first time, you will be asked to confirm GitHub’s fingerprint — type yes and press Enter. Then you should see:
Hi buckybadger! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.
That greeting (with your username) means everything works. The “does not provide shell access” part is expected and not an error — GitHub only uses this connection for Git, not for logging in.

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
text:
B.8 Troubleshooting
git@github.com: Permission denied (publickey)

The public key is not registered on GitHub, or you pasted the wrong one. Re-copy id_ed25519.pub (Step 4) and confirm it matches the key listed in GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys.

You are asked for your passphrase on every command

That is normal unless you set up the SSH agent (Step 3). Add the key to the agent to stop the repeated prompts.

Could not open a connection to your authentication agent

The agent is not running. Start it with eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" and then re-run ssh-add.

title: Appendix B — Setting Up SSH Keys
text:
B.9 You’re set
With ssh -T git@github.com greeting you by name, your computer and GitHub are linked. Head back to the Remotes in GitHub unit to connect your repository and push your first commits.

title: Appendix C — Using Meld for Diffs
text:
C.1 Step 1: Install Meld
The lessons show differences between versions of a file with git diff, which prints its output right in the terminal. That is quick for a line or two, but hard to read once changes get larger. Meld is a free, graphical diff tool that shows the two versions side by side, with changes highlighted and lined up — much easier to scan than terminal output.
This appendix installs Meld and sets it up as Git’s default difftool, so you can open any git diff in Meld instead. It is optional but recommended. Plan on about ten minutes.
Pick the instructions for your operating system, then confirm the install at the end.

title: Appendix C — Using Meld for Diffs
text:
C.1.1 Windows
Download the installer from meldmerge.org and run it. You can accept the defaults on every screen. The installer adds Meld to your PATH so that Git Bash can find it.


C.1.2 macOS
The simplest route is Homebrew:
brew install --cask meld
If you do not use Homebrew, download the .dmg from meldmerge.org and drag Meld into your Applications folder. (With the .dmg route, the meld command may not be on your PATH; Homebrew sets that up for you, which is why it is the easier option here.)


C.1.3 Linux
Install from your distribution’s package manager:
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install meld

# Fedora
sudo dnf install meld


C.1.4 Confirm it worked
In your terminal (Git Bash on Windows), check that Meld is on your PATH:
meld --version
meld 3.22.0
A version number means Git will be able to launch it.

title: Appendix C — Using Meld for Diffs
section: C.2 Step 2: Set Meld as Git’s difftool
text:
C.2 Step 2: Set Meld as Git’s difftool
Tell Git to use Meld whenever you run git difftool. These three commands write the settings to your global Git configuration, so you only do this once per computer:
git config --global diff.tool meld
git config --global difftool.prompt false
git config --global difftool.meld.cmd 'meld "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"'

diff.tool meld makes Meld the default difftool.
difftool.prompt false skips the “Launch meld?” confirmation before each file.
difftool.meld.cmd tells Git how to call Meld, with the two versions as its panes.







Note



Use single quotes around the cmd value. They keep $LOCAL and $REMOTE as literal text in your config file — Git fills them in with the actual file versions each time it runs.


These commands edit the .gitconfig file in your home folder. If you prefer to edit it by hand, the equivalent block is:
[diff]
    tool = meld
[difftool]
    prompt = false
[difftool "meld"]
    cmd = meld "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"

title: Appendix C — Using Meld for Diffs
text:
C.3 Step 3: Use it
Anywhere the lessons use git diff, you can swap in git difftool to open the comparison in Meld instead:







Command
What Meld shows




git difftool <file>
Your uncommitted copy vs. the last commit


git difftool <commit> <file>
A past version vs. your current copy


git difftool HEAD HEAD~2 <file>
The latest commit vs. two commits back


git difftool <hash1> <hash2> <file>
Two specific past versions, side by side



Meld opens a window with the two versions aligned. Close the window to return to the terminal; with difftool.prompt false set, Git moves on to the next file (if any) on its own.
Meld is also handy on its own, outside of Git: launch it and pick any two files to compare — for example, a document in your repo against an edited copy a collaborator emailed you.

title: Appendix C — Using Meld for Diffs
section: C.4 Optional: use Meld to resolve merge conflicts
text:
C.4 Optional: use Meld to resolve merge conflicts
Meld can also help with the merge conflicts from the Conflicts unit, showing your version, the incoming version, and the merged result together. To set it up as Git’s mergetool:
git config --global merge.tool meld
git config --global mergetool.prompt false
git config --global mergetool.meld.cmd 'meld "$LOCAL" "$MERGED" "$REMOTE" --output "$MERGED"'
Then, when a git pull or git merge reports a conflict, run:
git mergetool
Meld opens with the merged file in the center pane. Edit it until it reads how you want, save, and close. Then finish the merge the usual way with git add and git commit.

title: Appendix D — Git Cheatsheet
text:
A quick reference for every command in these lessons. Angle brackets like <file> mean “fill in your own value.”

D.0.1 The everyday rhythm
Most of your Git life is this short loop:
# before you start, get the latest
git pull origin main

# ... edit files ...

git add <file>            # stage your changes
git commit -m "message"   # save them to history
git push origin main      # send them to GitHub
Check in with git status any time you’re unsure where things stand.


D.0.2 One-time setup (per computer)







Command
What it does




git config --global user.name "Your Name"
Set the name stamped on your commits


git config --global user.email "you@wisc.edu"
Set the email on your commits (match GitHub)


git config --global core.editor "nano"
Use nano for commit messages (what these lessons assume)


git config --list
Show your current configuration


ssh -T git@github.com
Test that your SSH key connects to GitHub





D.0.3 Starting a repository



Command
What it does




git init
Turn the current folder into a Git repository


git clone <address>
Copy a GitHub repo onto this computer





D.0.4 The core cycle



Command
What it does




git status
Show untracked, modified, and staged files


git add <file>
Stage a file for the next commit


git add <file1> <file2>
Stage several files at once


git add .
Stage all changed files (run git status first!)


git commit -m "message"
Save all staged changes as a commit





D.0.5 Renaming and deleting files



Command
What it does




git mv <old> <new>
Rename or move a file, keeping its history


git rm <file>
Delete a tracked file (stages the deletion)



Both still need a git commit to record the change.


D.0.6 Seeing what changed







Command
What it does




git diff <file>
Changes since the last commit (not yet staged)


git diff --staged
Changes that are staged for the next commit


git diff HEAD <file>
All changes since the last commit


git diff <commit> <file>
Compare your file to a specific past commit


git log
Full commit history


git log --oneline
One compact line per commit


git log --oneline <file>
Only the commits that changed <file>


git log -2
Just the two most recent commits





D.0.7 Undoing and restoring







Command
What it does




git restore <file>
Discard uncommitted changes to a file


git restore --source=<commit> <file>
Bring back an older version of a file


git reset HEAD~1
Undo the last commit, keeping its changes in your files


git stash
Set aside uncommitted changes to return to later


git stash pop
Reapply the changes you stashed



Name a past commit with HEAD (latest), HEAD~1 (one before), and so on — or copy its ID from git log --oneline. Only git reset commits you have not yet pushed.


D.0.8 Ignoring files
Create a file named .gitignore and list patterns, one per line:
*.tmp          # any file ending in .tmp
receipts/      # a whole folder
secret.env     # a specific file



Command
What it does




git add .gitignore
Track the ignore file so the rules are shared


git add -f <file>
Force-add a file that is being ignored


git status --ignored
Also list the files being ignored





D.0.9 Working with GitHub







Command
What it does




git remote add origin <address>
Link your local repo to a GitHub repo


git remote -v
Show the remotes you’ve connected


git push origin main
Send your commits up to GitHub


git pull origin main
Bring GitHub’s changes down to your computer



After your first git push origin main, bare git push and git pull also work — but naming origin main keeps it unambiguous.


D.0.10 Key terms







Term
Meaning




Repository (repo)
A folder Git is tracking, plus its history


Commit
A saved snapshot of your project at a point in time


Staging area
Where changes wait after git add, before git commit


HEAD
The commit you’re currently on (usually the latest)


Remote
A named connection to a hosted copy (e.g. on GitHub)


origin
The conventional name for your main remote
